raw: P2JW285000-0-A00600-16D5D63078D A6 | Monday, October 12, 2026 THE WALL STREET JOURNAL U.S. NEWS # Probe of Trump Foes Falters Joe diGenova left the investigation last month. Departures, infighting, inexperience beset DOJ inquiry into alleged conspiracy Last year, Justice Department officials said an investigation would unravel a grand conspiracy by a cabal of national security officials who sought to undermine President Trump. By Sadie Gurman, Dave Michaels and Josh Dawsey Trump allies hoped it would confirm what they have been alleging for years: Officials who investigated the president over the past decade engaged in what was essentially a coordinated effort to violate his civil rights. Instead, the probe has been beset by departures, infighting and inexperience. The 81-year-old Reagan-era prosecutor coaxed out of retirement to lead the effort, Joe diGenova, quit last month, saying top department officials were pressuring the team to bring criminal cases before they were ready. He hadn't charged anyone. Officials denied pressuring him. DiGenova was one of several overlapping supervisors of the probe, with different interests and marching orders, adding to the chaotic nature of the effort. Last month, another senior counsel, Kurt Olsen, who had joined the probe from the White House, resigned from the inquiry, people familiar with the matter said. He had recently lost a security clearance after failing government polygraph tests about his foreign contacts. Olsen said the security clearance issue wasn't a factor in his departure but declined to elaborate. Trump is frustrated by the lack of progress and has complained about it to allies, a person familiar with the conversations said. Justice Department officials said the case is proceeding apace, with roughly a dozen prosecutors continuing to pursue a set of related investigations that could result in charges in coming weeks. But they privately acknowledge the idea of tying all those loose threads together in one big conspiracy case in South Florida, as they had initially attempted, isn't a practical approach. One of the officials said leadership is still confident in the people who continue to work on the inquiry, and recently brought on two former prosecutors. A White House spokeswoman said Trump has full confidence in Attorney General Todd Blanche to hold people accountable. In addition to the departures of Olsen and diGenova, Justice Department officials came to believe a third supervisor of the case, Miami U.S. attorney Jason Reding Quiñones, wasn't appropriately managing the investigation and his office more broadly. A number of the prosecutors on the probe complained to senior officials in Washington that Quiñones had given them no guidance, some of the people said. Lawyers in the deputy attorney general's office are now directly overseeing the Florida-based investigation from Washington, officials said. A spokeswoman for Quiñones defended his record on the job and said he was proud to serve in the Trump administration but declined to comment on the conspiracy investigation. The putative targets of the probe include a raft of people Trump has long disdained, including former CIA Director John Brennan, former FBI Director James Comey and officials involved in the August 2022 search of his Mar-a-Lago home. (Comey was separately charged in connection with a photo he posted of seashells that Trump alleged was threatening, and a judge dismissed a second case targeting him. He has denied the charges and said that there were an attempt at political retribution.) The investigation, which officials informally referred to as the grand-conspiracy probe, sought to tie together a series of past episodes, including the 2016 intelligence community assessment that Russia interfered in that year's election to boost Trump; the FBI's subsequent investigation into alleged Trump campaign ties to that Russian meddling; and the more recent criminal prosecutions by special counsel Jack Smith in 2023 and 2024 that stemmed from Trump's 2020 election loss. The probes went to two other U.S. attorneys before Quiñones raised his hand to oversee it, people familiar with the assignment said. One of the investigation's first targets: congressional testimony Brennan had given in 2017 and 2023 about the 2016 assessment. A veteran national-security prosecutor working on that line of inquiry, Maria Medets Long, soon told senior officials she hadn't found a basis to indict Brennan, some of the people said. In April, she was removed from the probe. The Justice Department had struggled to find and retain other prosecutors to work on it and brought on temporary hires; some of them had never worked as federal prosecutors. The office had to give them a crash course on presenting evidence to grand juries, some people familiar with the probe said. Justice Department officials in Washington at the time wanted prosecutors to speed up their process, including by subpoenaing witnesses to testify directly before a grand jury, without any FBI interview first, they said. Prosecutors usually avoid doing that to make sure they know what to expect a witness to say and avoid surprises before the grand jury. Prosecutors had to later withdraw the subpoenas after realizing information the witnesses would need to discuss with grand jurors was classified. Prosecutors had been trying to make the case that the FBI's court-authorized August 2022 search of Trump's Mar-a-Lago home, which led to charges that he illegally retained classified information, was unlawful. But an FBI agent told diGenova that tying the search to a broader conspiracy spanning from Florida to Washington would be challenging; diGenova disagreed and called FBI Director Kash Patel, who moved the agent off the investigation. # Jury Cases Attracting Online Bets Continued from Page One cial incentives to reach particular outcomes, no matter the facts of the case. Some court staffers are also potentially in positions to have inside knowledge of how deliberations are proceeding. The accessibility and pervasiveness of betting platforms makes the possibility of corrupting jurors a real risk, said University of Chicago law professor M. Todd Henderson. But there is a broader concern, he said, that prediction markets with heavy betting could influence how jurors think about a case. If millions are wagered on the belief that a defendant will be acquitted, could that make a jury more reluctant to convict? "For Joe Q. Juror sitting at home," Henderson said, "the question is: Is he likely to be more biased as a juror if he sees the odds on Polymarket than if he sees a pundit in the newspaper or on TV talking about what the chances are that Tyler Robinson did it?" Robinson's lawyers flagged the Polymarket bets to the presiding judge, arguing the wagering was a "morally dubious enterprise" that commodified death-penalty litigation. The defense said trading volume was active during a preliminary court hearing in July, and argued that continuing to broadcast the court proceedings would create additional pretrial publicity that was unfair to Robinson. "The Court credits Defendant's concerns regarding jury contamination and prediction-market activity as genuine," Judge Tony Graf wrote in a ruling last month. But he allowed continued livestreaming of the proceedings and suggested that any concerns could be addressed in jury selection, including by asking potential jurors about any exposure they had to prediction markets. Typically, markets for betting on criminal cases have been hosted on offshore platforms because prediction-market companies have wanted to avoid running afoul of U.S. rules that prohibit gambling on sensitive topics including war, terrorism and assassination. Still, market observers say that accessing the offshore platforms isn't difficult. Rutgers University statistics professor Harry Crane said around 20% to 40% of the money bet on offshore Polymarket markets comes from inside the U.S. The study doesn't show whether that volume comes from many people making small bets or a small number of super-users, said Crane, who serves on an advisory committee to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which regulates prediction markets. A Polymarket spokesperson said people "trade on outcomes of real-world events including legal, political and economic developments. These markets do not impact the outcomes—they reflect what market participants collectively believe will happen." Polymarket has a data partnership with Dow Jones, the publisher of The Wall Street Journal. At least a handful of courts are beginning to address the issue. The U.S. District Court in Chicago is updating its insider-trading policies to prohibit employees from using on-the-job information to make wagers. Judges in the district are on alert for similar concerns that might arise in jury trials, said Sean Lewis, a court spokesman. "As technology and society evolve, the court will continue to adapt its policies to safeguard the fair and impartial administration of justice," he said. The federal trial court in Manhattan has attracted at least two notable betting markets. Between May and July of last year, Polymarket users bet nearly $798,000 on the verdict of the Diddy sex trafficking trial. Combs was found not guilty of racketeering and sex-trafficking offenses but convicted of less serious charges. Maduro is set to go on trial next year in the same court, on charges including narcotics. A Polymarket offering on whether Maduro will be found guilty has attracted about $133,000 in trading volume so far.
